title: Where to Get a Michigan Medical Card: Steps and Costs
h1: Where to Get a Medical Card in Michigan, and What to Bring
metaDescription: Where to get a medical card in Michigan: finding a certifying physician, applying through the state registry, the $40 fee, what to bring, timing and renewals.

body:
Wondering where to get a medical card in Michigan? The card itself comes from the state. Michigan's Cannabis Regulatory Agency (CRA) runs the Michigan Medical Marijuana Program and issues registry cards after a Michigan physician certifies that you have a qualifying condition. Dispensaries, ours included, don't issue cards or certify patients. For a quick overview of the program, start with our [medical card page](/getting-a-medical-card/); below, you'll find who to see, what to bring, what it costs and how long it takes.

## Why some Michiganders still get a medical card

Adults 21 and older can already buy cannabis at adult-use stores with a valid ID, so a card isn't required to shop. People still register for a few reasons:

- **Age.** Michigan lets adults 18 and older register as patients.
- **Lower taxes.** Medical purchases by registered patients aren't subject to Michigan's 10% excise tax on adult-use cannabis; only the 6% sales tax applies.
- **Legal protection.** A valid registry card plus photo ID is what protects a patient from arrest under the medical law.
- **Caregivers.** A patient can name a registered caregiver, age 21 or older, to help.

A card is a legal status. It doesn't mean cannabis is right for your condition, so keep your doctor in the loop. Our guide to [Michigan medical card benefits](/blog/michigan-medical-marijuana-card-benefits/) weighs the trade-offs in detail.

## Where to get a medical card: Michigan physicians and the in-person question

Your first stop is a physician. The CRA says any medical doctor (MD), doctor of osteopathic medicine (DO) or Expedited Medical Compact physician licensed by the State of Michigan can sign the certification. That can be your own doctor or a physician at a clinic that does certifications.

The CRA's instructions call for a medical evaluation from an active Michigan physician within the last six months. Its guidance on third-party businesses goes further, telling applicants to have an in-person medical evaluation before the application is approved. Michigan's medical law also protects physicians only when they certify within a real physician-patient relationship, after a full review of your medical history.

So plan on an in-person visit. If a clinic offers a video visit instead, ask the CRA's medical program whether it meets the requirement before you pay.

### Qualifying conditions

Michigan's list of qualifying conditions includes:

- cancer, glaucoma, HIV/AIDS, hepatitis C and ALS
- Crohn's disease, colitis, inflammatory bowel disease and ulcerative colitis
- Alzheimer's agitation, Parkinson's disease, Tourette's disease, autism and cerebral palsy
- PTSD and OCD
- arthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, spinal cord injury, nail patella and chronic pain

It also covers a chronic or debilitating disease or medical condition, or its treatment, that produces cachexia or wasting syndrome, severe and chronic pain, severe nausea, seizures including epilepsy, or severe and persistent muscle spasms including multiple sclerosis. Your physician certifies the condition, and the CRA reviews the application.

## Finding a medical marijuana doctor in Michigan: choosing a reputable clinic

Certification clinics vary, so shop carefully:

- **Credentials.** Ask for the physician's name and check that they're an MD or DO licensed in Michigan.
- **Pricing.** Clinic fees are separate from the state's $40 application fee. Get the full price, including any follow-up visit, in writing.
- **Privacy.** Ask how your records are stored and whether they're shared with anyone.
- **The process.** A real evaluation reviews your medical history. Be wary of any business that promises approval.

One more warning sign comes straight from the CRA: businesses that tell patients their application and physician certification serve as a temporary registry card are putting those patients at risk of arrest. They don't. You also don't need a third-party service to apply, because you can file the application yourself.

## Your Michigan medical card application: online or on paper

The CRA runs the Michigan medical marijuana registry and offers two ways to apply:

- **Online**, through the CRA's portal, if you're a patient without a caregiver or you're removing your caregiver at renewal. This is the route for applying for a Michigan medical marijuana card online.
- **On paper**, using the CRA's application packet, if you have a caregiver or want to name one.

Send one complete application. The packet warns that any white-out or changes on the application or the physician certification form will lead to a denial, so fill out the forms carefully.

## What you need: ID, residency proof, certification and the fee

Before you apply, gather:

1. **Your physician certification**, completed and signed by your Michigan physician.
2. **Proof of Michigan residency.** Only Michigan residents can get a Michigan card. A Michigan driver's license or state ID works, or a voter registration card with proof of identity.
3. **The $40 application fee.** It's the same with or without a caregiver. Paper applications pay by check or money order.
4. **Caregiver details, if you're naming one.** A caregiver must be at least 21, consent to a criminal background check and have no disqualifying convictions.

## Step-by-step timeline

Here's how the process usually unfolds:

1. **Book a physician visit.** Bring records that document your condition.
2. **Get certified.** The physician completes the certification after evaluating you.
3. **Apply.** Submit online or on paper with the $40 fee.
4. **Wait for a decision.** The CRA must approve or deny an application within 15 business days. It has up to 20 business days from receiving it to issue a card or denial letter.
5. **Watch the mail.** The CRA suggests allowing 7 to 10 business days for mailing, and online applicants may receive a temporary registry card by email.
6. **Carry the real thing.** Until your card or temporary registry card arrives, your application and physician form don't count as a card.

## After approval: your card, caregivers and shopping at a provisioning center

Once you're approved, keep your registry card and a valid photo ID with you whenever you have cannabis, because legal protection depends on both. You'll also show both to shop as a patient at a licensed provisioning center, where Michigan limits patient purchases to 2.5 ounces a day and 10 ounces a month.

If you named a caregiver, they receive a separate caregiver card for you that expires on the same date as yours. Under Michigan law, a caregiver may assist up to five registered patients, and each patient may have only one caregiver.

Registered patients 18 and older with a valid card are welcome at High Society, and our [store locations page](/dispensary-locations/) lists every store. Our [patient guide](/patient-guide/) covers what to expect on a first visit, and our [Michigan cannabis FAQ](/blog/michigan-recreational-and-medical-cannabis-faq/) answers common medical-versus-adult-use questions. Ask your store about anything specific to patient purchases, and please consume responsibly.

## Medical card renewal in Michigan

A Michigan registry card is valid for two years. You can submit a renewal starting 90 days before your card expires, using the same application and the same $40 fee. Put the date on your calendar early, especially if you rely on a caregiver, since their card expires with yours. For possession limits and patient protections, see our [Michigan cannabis law guide](/cannabis-laws-by-state/michigan/).

faq.q: How much does a Michigan medical card cost?
faq.a: The state application fee is $40, and it's the same whether or not you name a caregiver. Renewal costs another $40 every two years. Separately, the physician or clinic that certifies you sets its own fee, which varies widely. Ask for the total price, including any follow-up visit, in writing before you book an appointment.

faq.q: Can a Michigan certification be done by video visit?
faq.a: Plan on an in-person visit. The CRA's guidance tells applicants to have an in-person medical evaluation from an active Michigan physician before the application is approved, and the certifying physician must be licensed in Michigan. If a clinic offers a video visit, ask the CRA's medical program whether it meets the requirement before you pay for it.

faq.q: How long does approval usually take?
faq.a: The CRA must approve or deny an application within 15 business days, and it has up to 20 business days to issue a card or denial letter. Add mail time on top; the CRA suggests allowing 7 to 10 business days for mailing. If you apply online, you may receive a temporary registry card by email while you wait for the card itself.

faq.q: How long does a Michigan card stay valid?
faq.a: Two years. You can submit a renewal starting 90 days before the expiration date, using the same application and the same $40 fee. If you have a caregiver, their card expires on the same day as yours, so renewing on time keeps both of you covered without a gap in your registration.

faq.q: Is a medical card required to shop at a Michigan dispensary?
faq.a: No, not for adults 21 and older, who need only a valid government-issued photo ID to shop adult-use. A card matters for adults 18 to 20, because registered patients 18 and older can buy with a valid card, and it also brings medical tax treatment and patient protections. High Society welcomes both adult-use customers and registered patients.
